strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem formulation: personalizing frozen VLAs to manipulate a specific user instance among visually similar distractors, a practically important and underexplored gap between category-level VLA generalization and instance-level control.

The proposed Visual Attentive Prompting (VAP) is simple, training-free, and modular, requiring no VLA fine-tuning or architectural changes, which makes it immediately deployable across different backbones (π_0, π_0.5) and robot embodiments.

Substantial benchmark contribution: two new simulation benchmarks (Personalized-SIMPLER across two robot platforms, Personalized-VLABench) plus a real-world SO-101 benchmark spanning selection and pick-and-place tasks over 8 object categories, filling a genuine gap since existing VLA benchmarks target category-level generalization.
Comprehensive empirical evaluation showing consistent, often large improvements over the generic VLA and language-based (hard/soft prompt) baselines across all benchmarks and metrics (SR and CMR).

Careful and honest baseline design: the token-learning (Yo'LLaVA-style) baseline is non-trivially adapted (with an embedding-space transfer analysis using cosine similarity/CKA/kNN and attention visualizations) to explain mechanistically why it underperforms VAP, which strengthens the scientific rigor of the comparison rather than using a strawman baseline.

Thorough error analysis (Appendix D) with a principled 3-way failure taxonomy (single-view grounding error, multi-view inconsistency, correct-prompt-but-failed-manipulation) supported by quantitative breakdowns and qualitative rollouts, giving an honest picture of where the method still struggles.
Runtime/efficiency analysis demonstrates the perception overhead is modest relative to VLA inference cost, supporting practical feasibility.
Extensive appendix material (training data construction, prompts used for LLM-generated descriptions, hyperparameters) aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: VAP is largely an engineering integration of existing off-the-shelf components (Grounding DINO, SAM2, DINOv2 embeddings, template-based instruction rewriting) rather than a new algorithmic contribution; the core idea of visual prompting to steer frozen policies is already established in prior work (e.g., MOKA, PIVOT, set-of-mark prompting), and the paper does not directly compare against these existing visual-prompting techniques for the personalization setting, only against text-based and token-learning baselines.

The per-view, independent grounding design is a clear robustness bottleneck: the authors' own error analysis shows multi-view inconsistency accounts for ~50-59% of failures in the multi-camera benchmarks, indicating the method's core weakness is not marginal but a dominant failure mode, and no cross-view consistency mechanism is proposed to mitigate it (deferred to future work).

The instruction-rewriting step relies on simple template-based string matching (e.g., replacing "my X" with a color-based generic phrase), which is brittle and was only demonstrated on a fixed personalized-instruction template; robustness to more naturalistic or varied phrasing of personalized requests is not evaluated.

Evaluation is restricted to short-horizon, single-personalized-object-per-scene tasks with only two same-category distractors; scalability to more distractors, multiple simultaneous personalized objects, or longer-horizon multi-step personalized tasks is untested, limiting evidence for broader applicability.

Real-world results are based on relatively few trials (20 per task) with no reported variance/error bars, making it harder to assess the statistical reliability of the reported success-rate differences.

No ablation isolating the contribution of individual VAP components (e.g., choice of highlight color/opacity, effect of using SAM2 tracking vs. re-grounding every frame, sensitivity to number/quality of reference images) beyond the qualitative embedding-space and error-case analyses, which would strengthen understanding of what specifically drives the gains.

strengths: Addresses a clearly motivated and practically important gap: existing VLA models cannot handle personalized/instance-level references (e.g., 'my cup') despite strong generic instruction-following ability.

VAP is simple, modular, and training-free, requiring only a handful of reference images per object and leaving the VLA backbone frozen — making it immediately deployable without costly per-object fine-tuning.

Thorough and diverse empirical evaluation: two new simulation benchmarks (Personalized-SIMPLER across Google Robot and WidowX, Personalized-VLABench on Franka) plus a real physical SO-101 robot setup with 8 object categories, covering both selection and pick-and-place tasks.

Strong and consistent quantitative gains over multiple well-constructed baselines (generic VLA, hard prompt with LLM-generated descriptions, and a carefully tuned token-learning/soft-prompt baseline inspired by Yo'LLaVA), across CMR and SR metrics.

The token-learning baseline is unusually rigorous: the authors verify the VLM-to-VLA embedding transfer assumption with cosine similarity/CKA/kNN analysis (Appendix B) and provide attention-heatmap visualizations showing why soft prompting fails to yield robust end-to-end control — this adds valuable mechanistic insight beyond a simple baseline comparison.

Detailed, honest error-case taxonomy (single-view grounding errors, multi-view inconsistency, correct-prompt-but-failed-manipulation) with quantitative breakdowns per benchmark, clarifying where the remaining bottlenecks lie.

Good reproducibility: extensive appendix with hardware/software details, training data construction, prompts used for baseline description generation, and runtime/efficiency analysis showing modest overhead (Table 5).
Clear, well-organized writing and figures that make the pipeline (grounding + visual prompting) easy to follow.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is modest: VAP largely composes existing off-the-shelf components (Grounding DINO for open-vocabulary detection, DINOv2 embeddings for instance matching, SAM2 for segmentation/tracking, and mask-based visual prompting akin to prior set-of-mark/visual-prompting work) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism.

No empirical comparison to other robotics-personalization systems mentioned in related work (e.g., PIN, MEMENTO, VLAS), so it is unclear how VAP compares to methods that also target personalized embodied instruction following, beyond the generic/hard/soft-prompt baselines constructed by the authors.

Cross-view inconsistency remains a large source of failure in multi-camera settings (59.2% of failures on Personalized-VLABench, 50.9% in real-world), indicating the per-view grounding design is not yet robust for practical multi-camera deployments — acknowledged but unresolved.
Evaluation is confined to a single VLA backbone family (π0/π0.5); generality of VAP as a plug-in adapter for other VLA architectures (OpenVLA, RT-2, Octo, etc.) is not empirically verified.

Real-world evaluation, while a valuable addition, is relatively small in scale (8 categories, 20 trials per task) and restricted to short-horizon, single-object tabletop tasks, limiting claims about broader applicability to cluttered, long-horizon, or multi-object personalization scenarios.

Performance is inherently bottlenecked by the quality of the frozen open-vocabulary detector and embedding matcher; for object categories or fine-grained distinctions poorly covered by Grounding DINO/DINOv2, grounding may fail regardless of the VLA's manipulation capability, and this dependency is not stress-tested with more adversarial or low-resource categories.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important gap: existing VLAs collapse personal/instance-level references (e.g., 'my cup') to category-level semantics, and the paper clearly formalizes this as a new 'personalized object manipulation' task.

The proposed method (Visual Attentive Prompting) is simple, training-free, and modular: it couples reference-based grounding (open-vocabulary detection + embedding matching + tracking) with a coupled visual-highlight/instruction-rewrite prompting strategy, requiring no modification of the frozen VLA backbone.

Extensive and diverse evaluation infrastructure: two new simulation benchmarks (Personalized-SIMPLER across Google Robot and WidowX, Personalized-VLABench on Franka) plus a real-world SO-101 tabletop benchmark spanning selection and pick-and-place tasks, demonstrating substantial engineering effort and broad applicability.

Strong, consistent empirical gains over multiple carefully constructed baselines (raw generic VLA, short/long hard text prompts, and a rigorously strengthened Yo'LLaVA-style token-learning soft-prompt baseline with oracle hard negatives), with the token baseline intentionally biased in its favor to make comparisons conservative.

Thorough ablation studies (necessity of instruction rewriting vs. mask alone, voting vs. averaging for reference aggregation, sensitivity to number of reference images, mask vs. bounding-box prompt geometry and opacity) that isolate the contribution of each design choice.

Honest and detailed failure-mode analysis (three failure categories with quantitative breakdowns per benchmark) that distinguishes grounding errors, multi-view inconsistency, and base-policy manipulation limitations, together with a well-articulated (if unimplemented) MAP-style cross-view association direction for future work.

Good reproducibility: extensive appendices document hardware/software, training data construction, hyperparameters, prompts used for generating textual descriptions, and runtime/efficiency analysis showing negligible overhead from the perception modules.
Additional real-world demonstration of multi-user/multi-object sequential personalization, showing the method's extensibility beyond the core single-object setting.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely an integration of existing off-the-shelf components (DINOv2, Grounding DINO, SAM2) with heuristic voting and template-based instruction rewriting rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic technique; novelty lies mainly in task framing and system design rather than methodology.

Multi-view inconsistency (Case 2) accounts for roughly 50-59% of remaining failures in Personalized-VLABench and real-world settings, and the paper only proposes this as an unimplemented future direction (Appendix D.2), leaving a substantial practical limitation unresolved in the current work.

A large fraction of residual failures (up to ~87% of failures in single-view Fractal/Bridge settings, and ~41-49% in multi-view settings) occur even when the object is correctly grounded and highlighted, indicating that much of the ceiling on performance is set by the base VLA's manipulation competence rather than by the proposed personalization mechanism, somewhat limiting the demonstrated significance of VAP itself.

The instruction-rewrite component is a rigid, deterministic rule-based template (mapping a possessive phrase to a canonical color word) rather than a more general or learned language-alignment mechanism; the claimed extensibility to LLM-based rewriting is mentioned but not empirically evaluated.

Benchmarks are authors' own adaptations of SIMPLER/VLABench with Sketchfab-sourced personal objects and constructed distractors, which, combined with real-world trials of modest scale (e.g., 20 trials per task), leaves some risk of evaluation-protocol bias or limited statistical power, despite reported error bars.

The overall system's reliability is tightly coupled to the quality of off-the-shelf open-vocabulary detectors/segmenters; there is limited discussion of behavior when the detector entirely fails to propose the correct object category or under objects far outside typical detector vocabularies.

strengths: Clearly motivated and well-formulated new task (instance-level 'personalized' object manipulation for VLAs), distinguishing it cleanly from standard category-level generalization studied in prior VLA work.

VAP itself is simple, training-free, and modular, operating purely at inference time on frozen backbones; Table 5 shows the perceptual overhead is negligible relative to VLA policy inference, which is practically appealing for deployment.

Substantial benchmark-building effort: two new simulation benchmarks (Personalized-SIMPLER across Google Robot/WidowX, Personalized-VLABench on Franka) plus a real-world SO-101 benchmark with selection and pick-and-place tasks, covering diverse robots, camera counts, and object categories.

Strong and consistent empirical gains over well-chosen baselines (raw generic VLA, short/long hard text prompts, and a carefully tuned token-learning 'soft prompt' baseline), with results reported for both success rate and a correct-object interaction metric (CMR) that helps separate grounding accuracy from execution capability.

The soft-prompt baseline is unusually rigorously validated: the authors verify via cosine similarity/CKA/kNN analysis (Appendix B) that the VLM-trained tokens transfer meaningfully into the VLA's embedding space, and provide attention-heatmap visualizations showing when/why token learning fails — this strengthens confidence that the comparison is fair rather than a strawman.

Thorough ablation studies (instruction rewriting vs. mask-only vs. rewrite-only, voting vs. averaging aggregation, sensitivity to number of reference images K, mask vs. bounding-box prompts, highlight opacity) isolate which design choices actually drive performance.

Honest and detailed failure-mode taxonomy (Appendix D, Table 9) that decomposes errors into single-view grounding mistakes, multi-view cross-camera inconsistency, and residual manipulation failures despite correct grounding, along with a concrete (if unimplemented) MAP-style formulation for future cross-view fusion work.

Additional real-robot demonstration of multi-user/multi-object scenarios (Appendix F) and general discussion of limitations/future directions (Appendix G) showing awareness of the method's current scope.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely an engineering pipeline combining existing off-the-shelf modules (Grounding DINO, DINOv2 matching, SAM2, and simple template-based instruction rewriting); the novelty lies primarily in the task formulation and benchmarks rather than in new algorithmic machinery.

Multi-view cross-camera inconsistency remains a major unsolved failure mode, accounting for roughly 50-59% of failures in the multi-view simulation and real-world benchmarks (Table 9); this limitation is explicitly acknowledged but not addressed empirically, only discussed as future work.

Overall performance, while much better than baselines, is still moderate in absolute terms (e.g., ~58.8% SR for real-world pick-and-place, ~65% two-step success in the multi-user extension), so the method does not fully close the gap to reliable personalized manipulation.

Method performance is fundamentally bottlenecked by the accuracy of frozen perception modules on novel, fine-grained instances; the paper does not stress-test grounding under harder distractor conditions (e.g., many more near-identical distractors, heavier occlusion) beyond the curated benchmark setups.

The rule-based instruction-rewrite scheme (parsing a fixed possessive template and substituting a color word) is somewhat brittle and template-specific; while the authors note it could be extended via LLM-based parsing, this extension is not implemented or evaluated.

No comparison to an oracle/fine-tuned upper bound (e.g., per-object fine-tuning) is provided to contextualize how much headroom remains between VAP and a fully specialized policy, despite the paper's claim that such fine-tuning is impractical.

Simulation benchmarks rely on a fairly limited number of object categories (2-8 depending on setting) built from Sketchfab assets, which may not fully capture the visual diversity and fine-grained similarity of real personal belongings encountered in practice.
